front_blocks.md: Define **acyl chloride**.

back_blocks.md: An **acyl chloride** is a carboxylic acid derivative in which the –OH group is replaced by –Cl, making it highly reactive towards nucleophilic addition-elimination reactions.

cards.front_md: Define **acyl chloride**.

front_blocks.md: What reagents convert a carboxylic acid into an acyl chloride, and what by-products does each produce?

back_blocks.md: Three reagents work: **PCl**<sub>**5**</sub> (solid) gives POCl<sub>3</sub> and HCl; **PCl**<sub>**3**</sub> (liquid, heat) gives H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub>; **SOCl**<sub>**2**</sub> (liquid) gives SO<sub>2</sub> and HCl.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Phenol reacts with carboxylic acids to form esters at a fast rate without any additional reagents.

back_blocks.md: **False.** The esterification of phenol with carboxylic acids is slow, so **acyl chlorides** are used instead to give a faster, higher-yield reaction.

front_blocks.md: Benzoic acid is produced from methylbenzene in two steps: first, refluxing with hot alkaline **..........**; second, treatment with dilute **..........**.

back_blocks.md: Benzoic acid is produced from methylbenzene in two steps: first, refluxing with hot alkaline **KMnO**<sub>**4**</sub>; second, treatment with dilute **HCl**.

front_blocks.md: How are non-substituted and substituted amides distinguished by the reagent used with an acyl chloride?

back_blocks.md: A **non-substituted amide** is formed by reaction with **ammonia (NH**<sub>**3**</sub>**)**. A **substituted amide** is formed by reaction with a **primary amine**, via nucleophilic addition-elimination.

front_blocks.md: Define **electrophile**.

back_blocks.md: An **electrophile** is an electron-pair acceptor, a species that attacks regions of high electron density such as the delocalised π system of arenes during electrophilic substitution reactions.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Phenol reacts with bromine water at room temperature to form a white precipitate.

back_blocks.md: **True.** **Phenol** undergoes electrophilic substitution with bromine water at room temperature, forming a white precipitate of **2,4,6-tribromophenol**.

front_blocks.md: When phenol reacts with dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> at room temperature, the products are a mixture of **..........**-nitrophenol and **..........**-nitrophenol.

back_blocks.md: When phenol reacts with dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> at room temperature, the products are a mixture of **2**-nitrophenol and **4**-nitrophenol.

front_blocks.md: What electrophile is involved in the nitration of benzene, and how is it generated?

back_blocks.md: The electrophile is the **nitronium ion, NO**<sub>**2**</sub><sup>**+**</sup>. It is generated by mixing concentrated **HNO**<sub>**3**</sub> and concentrated **H**<sub>**2**</sub>**SO**<sub>**4**</sub>, where the sulfuric acid protonates the nitric acid.

back_blocks.md: **KCN in ethanol** is used in a **nucleophilic substitution** reaction. It is useful because it increases the carbon chain length by one, allowing longer-chain target molecules to be reached.

back_blocks.md: **Ammonia (NH**<sub>**3**</sub>**)** reacts with an acyl chloride in a **nucleophilic addition-elimination** reaction to form a **primary amide** and hydrogen chloride gas.

front_blocks.md: Define **elimination reaction**.

back_blocks.md: An **elimination reaction** is one in which atoms or groups are removed from adjacent carbons to form a double bond. For example, dehydration of an alcohol produces an alkene.

front_blocks.md: What reagents and conditions convert benzene into phenylethanone (acetophenone)?

back_blocks.md: **CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**COCl** and **AlCl**<sub>**3**</sub> are used in a **Friedel-Crafts acylation** (electrophilic substitution). AlCl<sub>3</sub> acts as a Lewis acid catalyst to generate the acylium ion RCO<sup>+</sup>.

front_blocks.md: An ester can be hydrolysed in two ways: **acid hydrolysis** with dilute acid gives a **..........** ; **alkaline hydrolysis** with NaOH (aq) gives a **carboxylate salt** and an **..........** .

back_blocks.md: An ester can be hydrolysed in two ways. **Acid hydrolysis** with dilute acid gives a **carboxylic acid**. **Alkaline hydrolysis** with NaOH (aq) gives a **carboxylate salt** and an **alcohol**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A ketone can be reduced to a secondary alcohol using NaBH<sub>4</sub> in water.

back_blocks.md: **True.** **Ketones** are reduced to **secondary alcohols** using **NaBH**<sub>**4**</sub> in water — the hydride ion acts as a nucleophile, reducing the C=O group.

H<sub>2</sub> with a Pt catalyst will reduce both the benzene ring and the COOH group in a benzoic acid derivative.

back_blocks.md: **False.** Under **hydrogenation** conditions (H<sub>2</sub>/Pt or Ni), the **benzene ring** is reduced to cyclohexane. The **–COOH group** is typically not reduced under these conditions.

front_blocks.md: Why is it more effective to synthesise an ester from an acyl chloride rather than directly from a carboxylic acid and alcohol?

back_blocks.md: The acyl chloride is **more reactive**, so the reaction goes to **completion** and gives a **higher yield**, whereas direct esterification with a carboxylic acid is reversible and slow.

front_blocks.md: What is the by-product when a carboxylic acid is reduced to a primary alcohol?

back_blocks.md: The by-product is **water (H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O)**. The reduction of the –COOH group to –CH<sub>2</sub>OH removes an oxygen atom, which leaves as water.
